entries.title: Roast and baste
entries.say: As it reads: roast and baste.
entries.summary: Roasting cooks meat or poultry in the dry heat of an oven: high heat to brown the outside, lower heat to cook it through. Basting adds colour and flavour, and resting lets carryover heat finish the centre.
entries.guest: Roasted means cooked in the dry heat of the oven, browned outside and rested so it stays juicy. Our Chateaubriand is roasted whole for two, so it takes longer than a steak.

paras: Roasting is cooking by dry heat in an oven. Hot air and the heat thrown off the oven walls brown the outside of a joint, a large piece of meat, or a whole bird, while heat travels slowly inward to cook the centre. No liquid goes in the pan, which is what separates a roast from a braise. The browning is the Maillard reaction, the chemistry behind a seared crust, and it is where most of a roast's flavour comes from. In the classical brigade the rôtisseur ran the roasts, and often the grill and fryer too.

Season ahead. Salt a large joint or a whole bird the day before, about 10 g (0.35 oz) of fine salt for each 1 kg (2.2 lb), and leave it uncovered in the fridge: the salt seasons deeper as it is drawn back into the meat, and the dry surface browns better. Take the chill off for 30 minutes to an hour before cooking, within the kitchen's time rules. Tie a joint into an even shape so it cooks at one rate, and set it on a rack or a bed of bones and vegetables so hot air reaches underneath.

The classic roast starts hot, about 220°C (428°F), for 15 to 20 minutes to brown, then drops to about 160°C (320°F) to cook through gently. Searing first in a hot pan does the same browning on the stove. Many cooks now reverse the order: roast low, about 120°C (248°F), until the centre is nearly there, then brown hard at the end. This reverse sear gives meat that is pink almost to the edge, with only a thin grey band under the crust.

Baste as it roasts. Every 15 to 20 minutes, tip the pan and spoon its hot fat and juices over the meat; the French word is arroser, to water. Basting colours and flavours the surface and keeps lean skin from drying, but it does not push juice into the meat, and every opening of the door costs the oven heat, so baste quickly.

Carryover is heat still travelling inward after the roast leaves the oven. The outside is far hotter than the centre, so the centre keeps climbing: a beef tenderloin taken out at 52°C (126°F) for medium-rare rises to about 55 to 57°C (131 to 135°F) as it rests. That is why a roast comes out before it reaches its target. Beef served below 63°C (145°F), the figure food safety charts give for whole cuts, is covered by the consumer advisory on undercooked meat.

Rest the roast on a rack in a warm place, loosely covered, for 10 to 20 minutes for a large joint and about 5 for a duck breast, then carve across the grain. Resting lets the juices settle and thicken a little, so they stay in the slice instead of flooding the board.

Judge doneness with a probe thermometer pushed into the thickest part, away from bone, and check more than one spot. A whole chicken is read in the thickest part of the thigh and must reach 74°C (165°F). Touch helps on small cuts: raw meat is soft and firms as it cooks, so an experienced cook can press a steak and know it. A roast is too big to judge that way; the probe decides.

At Brennan's the Roasted Chateaubriand is the centre cut of a Creekstone Farms tenderloin, roasted whole for two so it stays juicy; its sauce and plate are taught in their own entry. The Roasted Rohan Duck Breast, the fourth course of the dinner tasting, is roasted so the skin renders and the meat stays rosy; a duck breast is classically scored, rendered skin down, finished in the oven, rested and sliced across the grain, and the kitchen's own steps are confirmed at lineup.

The kitchen and the ticket speak of doneness in words, rare, medium-rare, medium, medium-well and well done, each a band on the chef's chart, taught in Cooking terms on the ticket. Write the guest's word exactly, and for the Chateaubriand ask once for the whole table, since one roast serves both. Tell the table at the order that a whole roast takes longer than a steak, and ask at lineup where it is carved tonight. The duck is usually served medium-rare to medium: confirm the kitchen's standard and tonight's garnish at lineup before you describe it.

faults.fault: Thick grey band under the crust
faults.cause: The oven ran too hot for too long, or a cold joint had a long, hard sear.
faults.fix: Roast lower and longer, or reverse the order: a low oven first and a hard sear at the end.

faults.cause: A wet surface, a cool oven, or a bird sitting in its own juices.
faults.fix: Salt ahead and dry it uncovered in the fridge, start hot, and roast on a rack.

faults.cause: Taken out at the target temperature, with nothing allowed for carryover.
faults.fix: Take it out a few degrees early and let the rest finish it.

faults.cause: Carved straight from the oven.
faults.fix: Rest it on a rack, loosely covered, before carving across the grain.

faults.cause: A joint straight from the fridge, or one uneven in shape.
faults.fix: Take the chill off first and tie it into an even shape.

faults.cause: An empty pan under high heat.
faults.fix: Roast on a bed of bones and vegetables, or add a splash of water to the pan.

cards.front: What separates roasting from braising?
cards.back: Roasting is dry heat in an oven with no liquid in the pan; a braise cooks partly covered in liquid, low and slow.

cards.front: Why does a classic roast start hot and then drop the heat?
cards.back: The high heat, about 220°C (428°F), browns the outside for flavour; the lower heat, about 160°C (320°F), cooks the centre through evenly.

cards.front: What is a reverse sear, and what does it give?
cards.back: Roast low first, then brown hard at the end: meat pink almost to the edge, with only a thin grey band under the crust.

cards.front: Why salt a roast the day before?
cards.back: The salt seasons deeper as it is drawn back into the meat, and the surface dries uncovered in the fridge, so it browns better.

cards.front: What does basting do, and what does it not do?
cards.back: Spooning hot fat and juices over the meat colours and flavours the surface; it does not push juice inside, and every opening of the door costs heat.

cards.front: What is carryover heat?
cards.back: Heat still moving inward after the roast leaves the oven, so the centre keeps climbing as it rests. A roast comes out before its target.

cards.front: When does a tenderloin come out for medium-rare, and where does it finish?
cards.back: It comes out at about 52°C (126°F) and rises to about 55 to 57°C (131 to 135°F) as it rests.

cards.front: Why does a roast rest before carving?
cards.back: The juices settle and thicken a little, so they stay in the slice instead of running across the board.

cards.front: How do you read a roast's doneness?
cards.back: With a probe thermometer in the thickest part, away from bone, checked in more than one place. Touch works on small cuts, never on a roast.

cards.front: Where and to what temperature is a whole roast chicken checked?
cards.back: In the thickest part of the thigh, the slowest part of the bird to cook, to 74°C (165°F).

cards.front: What does a table ordering the Chateaubriand need to hear?
cards.back: It is the centre of the tenderloin roasted whole for two, it takes longer than a steak, and it needs one temperature for the table.

cards.front: How is the Rohan duck breast roasted and served?
cards.back: Roasted so the skin renders and the meat stays rosy, usually medium-rare to medium; the kitchen's steps and standard are confirmed at lineup.

questions.q: Why does a classic roast begin in a hot oven before the heat is lowered?
questions.answer: To brown the outside for flavour
distractors: To seal the juices inside the meat
To cook the centre faster
To melt the salt into the skin
questions.why: High heat drives the browning that gives a roast its flavour. Searing does not seal in juice, and the lower heat then cooks the centre evenly.

questions.q: A roast reaches its target temperature in the oven and comes out at that moment. What happens next?
questions.answer: Carryover takes it past the target
distractors: It holds at the target as it rests
It cools below the target at once
Its juices seal in and it stays rare
questions.why: The outside is hotter than the centre, so heat keeps moving inward after the oven. A roast comes out a few degrees early.

questions.q: At about what centre temperature does a beef tenderloin come out of the oven for medium-rare?
questions.why: Taken out at about 52°C (126°F), it climbs to about 55 to 57°C (131 to 135°F) as it rests; 74°C (165°F) is the figure for poultry.

questions.q: Which method gives a roast that is pink almost to the edge, with only a thin grey band?
questions.answer: Roast low first, then sear hard at the end
distractors: Sear hard first, then roast very hot
Roast covered in stock, then grill it
Roast hot throughout, basting every minute
questions.why: Low heat cooks the meat evenly from edge to centre, and the final hard sear browns only the surface, so the grey band stays thin.

questions.q: What does basting a roast with its own fat and juices actually achieve?
questions.answer: Colour and flavour on the surface
distractors: Juice pushed deep into the meat
A faster cook with the door open
A sealed crust that holds in juice
questions.why: Basting browns and flavours the outside and keeps lean skin from drying. It cannot drive moisture into the meat, and opening the door costs heat.

questions.q: Why is a roast rested before it is carved?
questions.answer: The juices settle and stay in the slice
distractors: The fat sets so it can be trimmed
The crust softens for easier carving
The meat cools enough to plate cold
questions.why: Resting lets the juices settle and thicken slightly while carryover finishes the centre, so less runs onto the board.

questions.q: Where is a whole roast chicken checked, and to what temperature?
questions.answer: The thickest part of the thigh, 74°C (165°F)
distractors: The thickest part of the thigh, 63°C (145°F)
The thickest part of the breast, 57°C (135°F)
Just inside the cavity, 74°C (165°F)
questions.why: The thigh is the thickest, slowest part of the bird to cook, and poultry must reach 74°C (165°F) there.

questions.q: A couple orders the Roasted Chateaubriand. What should the server do when taking the order?
questions.answer: Take one temperature and mention the timing
distractors: Take two temperatures, one for each guest
Promise it in the time of a single steak
Ask the kitchen to slice it before roasting
questions.why: One whole roast serves both guests, so it takes one temperature, and a whole roast takes longer than a steak, so the table hears it at the order.

questions.q: How is the Roasted Rohan Duck Breast usually served at Brennan's?
questions.answer: Rosy, usually medium-rare to medium
distractors: Well done, so the fat renders fully
Rare and cold, sliced like carpaccio
As confit, cooked slowly in its own fat
questions.why: Roasted so the skin renders, the breast is served rosy; the kitchen's standard is confirmed at lineup, and the confit leg belongs to the waffle.

entries.title: Grill and salamander
entries.say: As it reads: grill and salamander.
entries.summary: Grilling cooks food on bars over heat from below, marking it and flavouring it with smoke from the dripping fat. The salamander is the professional kitchen's overhead grill (broiler): fierce heat from above for finishing, glazing and gratins.
entries.guest: Grilled means cooked on bars over a flame, for dark marks and a smoky edge. A gratin's golden top comes from a moment under fierce heat from above.

paras: Grilling is cooking on metal bars over heat from below: glowing charcoal, gas burners or burning wood. The heat reaches the food two ways, as radiant heat from the fire and by direct contact with the hot bars, which brand dark lines into the surface. Fat and juices drip onto the heat, smoke and sometimes flare, and that smoke is part of the flavour. It is fast, fierce heat, so it suits tender, fairly thin food: steaks, chops, fish, shrimp, vegetables and split chicken.

The salamander turns the fire upside down. It is a gas or electric element above a rack that can be raised or lowered, usually mounted over the range. It gives fierce heat from above for seconds or a minute or two: to brown a gratin, glaze a sauce, melt cheese or finish a dish that is already cooked. The name comes from an old kitchen tool, an iron plate on a long handle heated in the fire and held over a dish to brown it, itself named for the creature that legend said could live in flames.

Build zones. On a charcoal grill, bank the coals deep on one side and thin on the other; on gas, set one burner high and one low. The hot zone, about 260°C (500°F) at the bars, marks and sears; the cooler zone, around 175°C (347°F), finishes thick pieces gently, lid down, without burning the outside. A cook can read the heat with a hand held about 12 cm (5 inches) above the bars: two or three seconds before it must come away means hot, five or six means medium.

Mark and turn. Scrape the bars clean and heat them well, dry the food and brush it lightly with oil, then lay it down and leave it: it sticks until a crust forms, then lets go. For crosshatched marks, the French quadrillage, give the piece a quarter turn on the same side after a minute or two, then turn it over and finish. Move anything that flares to the cooler zone rather than drowning the flames.

Under the salamander, heat the dish through first, in the oven or on the stove, because the salamander only colours: a cold gratin burns on top and stays cold beneath. Then set the rack close and watch every second. A Mornay gratin, vegetables or pasta under a béchamel enriched with cheese, bubbles and browns in a minute or two. A sabayon, egg yolks whisked with wine and sugar to a warm foam and spooned over fruit, takes colour in seconds and catches if you turn away. Oysters Rockefeller, on the half shell under a rich green topping, need fierce top heat so the topping bubbles before the oysters overcook.

Chargrilled oysters are the modern New Orleans classic of the grill. At Drago's in Metairie, Tommy Cvitanovich began cooking oysters on the half shell over a hot grill in 1993, under garlic butter, herbs and grated Parmesan and Romano. The butter bubbles and flares, the edges of the oysters curl, and French bread on the side mops up the butter. Drago's calls them charbroiled oysters, and the dish has spread across the city.

For a guest, grilled means bars and a flame: a smoky edge and dark marks. A gratin or a glazed sauce has met the salamander for its golden top. Blackening is neither: it is a spiced crust cooked in a very hot iron pan, taught in its own entry. And an American grilled cheese sandwich is usually toasted in a pan or on a flat griddle, whatever its name says.

British English says grill for both: food goes on the grill, over the heat, or under the grill, beneath it. An American kitchen keeps grill for heat from below and gives the overhead grill (broiler) its own name. Professional kitchens on both sides of the Atlantic call their version the salamander.

ratios.label: The hand test
ratios.value: A hand about 12 cm (5 inches) above the bars: two or three seconds is hot, five or six is medium

ratios.label: Crosshatched marks
ratios.value: A quarter turn on the same side after a minute or two, then turn it over once

temps.label: Hot zone at the bars, to mark and sear
Cooler zone, to finish thick pieces

faults.cause: Dirty or cool bars, wet food, or turned before the crust formed.
faults.fix: Scrape and heat the bars, dry and lightly oil the food, and wait until it lets go.

faults.cause: Fat dripping onto a fierce fire, or old fat burning on the bars.
faults.fix: Trim excess fat, move the piece to the cooler zone and keep the bars clean.

faults.cause: A thick piece left on the hot zone.
faults.fix: Mark it on the hot side, then finish it on the cooler side under the lid or in the oven.

faults.fault: Gratin burnt on top, cold beneath
faults.cause: The dish went under the salamander cold, or too close to the element.
faults.fix: Heat it through first and use the salamander only for colour.

faults.cause: A sabayon or sauce left under the heat too long.
faults.fix: Watch it every second and pull it the moment it colours.

cards.front: Where does the heat come from when you grill?
cards.back: From below: coals, gas or wood, as radiant heat and by contact with the hot bars, which mark the food.

cards.front: Why does grilled food taste smoky even over gas?
cards.back: Fat and juices drip onto the heat and smoke, and that smoke flavours the food; too much and it flares and turns sooty.

cards.front: What is a salamander in a professional kitchen?
cards.back: The overhead grill (broiler): an element above a rack that can be raised or lowered, giving fierce heat from above for browning, glazing and gratins.

cards.front: Where does the salamander get its name?
cards.back: From an old iron plate on a long handle, heated in the fire and held over a dish to brown it, named for the creature said to live in flames.

cards.front: Why build a hot zone and a cooler zone on a grill?
cards.back: The hot zone marks and sears; the cooler zone finishes thick pieces gently without burning the outside, and gives flare-ups somewhere to go.

cards.front: Why leave food alone when it first goes on the grill?
cards.back: It sticks until a crust forms, then lets go of clean, hot, oiled bars. Moved too soon, it tears.

cards.front: How do you make crosshatched grill marks?
cards.back: Lay the piece down, give it a quarter turn on the same side after a minute or two, then turn it over and finish.

cards.front: Why is a gratin heated through before it goes under the salamander?
cards.back: The salamander only colours. A cold dish burns on top before its centre is hot.

cards.front: Name three jobs for the salamander.
cards.back: Browning a Mornay gratin, glazing a sabayon over fruit, and finishing Oysters Rockefeller until the topping bubbles.

cards.front: Which restaurant is credited with chargrilled oysters, and when?
cards.back: Drago's in Metairie, where Tommy Cvitanovich first grilled oysters on the half shell with garlic butter, herbs and grated cheese in 1993.

cards.front: Why do British and American cooks mean different things by grill?
cards.back: British English uses grill for heat from above and below; an American kitchen keeps grill for heat from below and names the overhead grill (broiler) separately.

cards.front: Is blackened fish grilled?
cards.back: No: blackening is a spiced crust cooked in a very hot iron pan, a method with its own entry.

questions.q: In a professional kitchen, what is the salamander?
questions.answer: An overhead grill giving fierce heat from above
distractors: A charcoal grill giving fierce heat from beneath
A deep fryer kept for small fish
A low oven for holding plates warm
questions.why: The salamander sits above a rack that can be raised or lowered, and browns, glazes and gratinates from above in seconds or minutes.

questions.q: Why does a cook set up a hot zone and a cooler zone on a grill?
questions.answer: To mark on one and finish gently on the other
distractors: To grill meat and fish at the same time
To stop the fat from dripping at all
To smoke on one side and fry on the other
questions.why: Thick pieces are marked on the hot side, then finished on the cooler side so the outside does not burn before the centre cooks.

questions.q: A steak sticks to the grill bars when you try to turn it after a few seconds. What should you do?
questions.answer: Leave it until a crust forms and it lets go
distractors: Pour oil over the bars beneath it
Scrape it off with a sharp spatula
Turn up the heat so it loosens
questions.why: Food sticks until its surface browns into a crust; on clean, hot, oiled bars it then lets go cleanly.

questions.q: A gratin goes under the salamander straight from the fridge. What happens?
questions.answer: It burns on top and stays cold beneath
distractors: It heats evenly from the bottom up
Its cheese melts but will not brown
Its sauce thickens without colouring
questions.why: The salamander only colours the surface, so a dish is heated through in the oven or on the stove before it goes under.

questions.q: Which restaurant is credited with chargrilled oysters, first grilled there in 1993?
questions.answer: Drago's
distractors: Antoine's
Galatoire's
Commander's Palace
questions.why: Tommy Cvitanovich first grilled oysters with garlic butter and cheese at Drago's in Metairie in 1993; Drago's calls them charbroiled oysters.

questions.q: A British recipe says to finish a dish under the grill. What does an American cook reach for?
questions.answer: The overhead grill (broiler)
distractors: The charcoal grill outside
The flat griddle
The deep fryer
questions.why: British English says grill for heat from above as well as below; an American kitchen names the overhead grill (broiler) separately.

questions.q: Where does most of the smoky flavour of gas-grilled food come from?
questions.answer: Fat and juices dripping onto the heat
distractors: The gas itself as it burns
Smoke given off by the hot metal bars
Salt burning on the surface
questions.why: Drippings hit the hot burners and smoke, and that smoke rises into the food; too much fat flares and turns sooty.

questions.q: Which of these is finished under the salamander?
questions.answer: A Mornay gratin
distractors: A beurre blanc
A poached egg
A court-bouillon
questions.why: A gratin under cheese sauce is browned by fierce top heat; a butter sauce would split, and the others need no colour.

entries.title: Smoking, hot and cold
entries.summary: Smoking flavours food with the smoke of smouldering wood. Hot smoking cooks as it flavours, as with andouille and tasso; cold smoking flavours without cooking and always follows a cure. Today smoke is mostly a seasoning.
entries.guest: Our Smoked Cauliflower is smoked for a deep, savoury flavour, then brightened with preserved lemon and a moderate warmth from harissa.

paras: Smoke is what wood gives off when it smoulders, burning slowly with too little air to flame. Heated wood breaks down into hundreds of compounds: some give the smoky, spicy aroma, others react on the surface of the food to give a mahogany colour, and some slow the growth of bacteria and the spoiling of fat. Smoke works on the surface, so a dry, slightly tacky skin, the pellicle, takes it best.

For most of history smoke was a preserver, working with salt and drying to keep meat and fish through lean months. Refrigeration took over that job, and smoke today is chiefly a flavour, but the old order stands: salt first, then smoke.

Hot smoking cooks as it smokes. The food sits in a closed smoker or smokehouse over smouldering wood, at a heat high enough to cook it through, slowly. Andouille, tasso and the smoked sausage of south Louisiana are hot smoked, each cured or seasoned first; so are hot-smoked salmon and trout, which flake when done. Bacon is smoked warm too, but it is still cooked before it is eaten. Rules for hot-smoked fish commonly ask for the centre to be held at 63°C (145°F) or more for at least 30 minutes.

Cold smoking flavours without cooking. The smoke is made apart from the food and cooled before it reaches it, and the chamber is kept below about 32°C (90°F), the ceiling smoked seafood guidelines set, so the flesh does not cook: smoked salmon stays silky, cheese stays whole, and some hams take smoke for days. That warmth is no barrier to bacteria, so cold smoking always follows a cure: salmon is salted, often with sugar, rinsed and air-dried to a pellicle before the smoke.

Choose the wood. Hardwoods give clean smoke: hickory strong and bacon-like; pecan, a kind of hickory, milder and sweeter; oak steady and medium; fruitwoods such as apple and cherry gentle and sweet. Resinous softwoods like pine and spruce give a bitter, sooty smoke and are never used. The wood should be dry and seasoned and the smoke thin and pale blue; thick white smoke from a smothered fire coats food with acrid soot.

Smoke at the pass is a seasoning, not a preserver. A smoking gun burns a pinch of wood chips and blows cool smoke through a tube under a glass cloche, over a plate, a cocktail or a container of liquid, for a few seconds to a few minutes. Liquids, purées and dressings take smoke quickly, and a little goes a long way.

In south Louisiana the smokehouse and the boucherie belong together. A boucherie is a communal hog butchering, Cajun and Creole alike, born before refrigeration and still held in rural communities, where families and neighbours work together to turn a whole hog into food: boudin, cracklins, hogshead cheese, andouille and more. In those days, meat that could not be eaten fresh was salted, made into sausage and smoked to keep, which is why the two are remembered together in rural south Louisiana.

At Brennan's smoke turns up as a seasoning across the menus: the smoked tomato water poured last over the Creole Tomato Tostada, the smoked oyster dressing of the Creole Caesar, the smoked potato pavé beside the breakfast hanger steak, and the Smoked Cauliflower side at dinner, finished with preserved lemon and harissa. How each one is smoked is the kitchen's detail.

Tell guests where the smoke is before it surprises them. The Creole Caesar's dressing is made with smoked oysters: mention it to every guest, flag it on the ticket and take any shellfish question to the kitchen. Describe smoke as a gentle, savoury note rather than barbecue, and leave the method to the chef.

temps.label: Hot-smoked fish: the centre held at least 30 minutes at or above
Cold smoking: the chamber stays below

faults.cause: Thick white smoke from a smothered fire, damp or resinous wood, or too long in the smoke.
faults.fix: Use dry hardwood, let the fire breathe for thin blue smoke, and smoke for less time.

faults.cause: A wet surface with no pellicle.
faults.fix: Air-dry the food until its surface is tacky before it goes in.

faults.fault: Cold-smoked fish turned opaque and soft
faults.cause: The chamber ran too warm and began to cook it.
faults.fix: Keep the smoke cool, below about 32°C (90°F), and smoke in cool weather or over ice.

faults.cause: Too long under the cloche, or a liquid smoked too heavily.
faults.fix: Smoke briefly and taste, or blend a smoked portion back into an unsmoked one.

components: Okra tostada and smoked tomato water
brennans.how: Tomato water, the clear juice of salted, puréed tomatoes hung overnight, is smoked for a gentle campfire note and poured on last, so the okra tostada stays crisp for the first bites. Questions about the tostada itself go to the kitchen.

Smoked oysters are blended into the Caesar dressing, taking the briny role anchovy usually plays, with a gentle smoke. Tell every guest, flag it on the ticket and take shellfish questions to the kitchen.

The potato pavé beside the hanger steak carries a smoky note. Whether the smoke is in the cream, the butter or the finished block is the kitchen's detail, so call it smoky and leave the method to the chef.
Smoked for a deep, savoury flavour, then finished with preserved lemon and harissa for brightness and a moderate warmth. Whether the side is cooked with butter or oil is a question for the kitchen.

cards.front: What does smoke come from, and why does the fire not flame?
cards.back: Wood smouldering with too little air to flame; heated slowly, it breaks down into compounds that colour, flavour and help preserve the food.

cards.front: Where does smoke flavour food, and what helps it take?
cards.back: On the surface. A dry, slightly tacky skin called the pellicle takes smoke evenly and well.

cards.front: What is hot smoking?
cards.back: Smoking at a heat that cooks the food through as it flavours it: andouille, tasso and hot-smoked fish that flakes.

cards.front: What centre temperature and time do rules commonly set for hot-smoked fish?
cards.back: At least 63°C (145°F) at the centre, held there for at least 30 minutes.

cards.front: What is cold smoking, and what is it used for?
cards.back: Smoking with the chamber below about 32°C (90°F), so the food takes flavour without cooking: smoked salmon, cheese and some hams.

cards.front: Why does cold smoking always follow a cure?
cards.back: Cold smoke does not cook, and its warmth suits bacteria, so the salt does the protecting and the smoke adds flavour.

cards.front: Which woods give good smoke, and which are never used?
cards.back: Hardwoods such as hickory, pecan, oak, apple and cherry; never resinous softwoods like pine, which give a bitter, sooty smoke.

cards.front: What should good smoke look like?
cards.back: Thin and pale blue. Thick white smoke from a smothered fire coats food with acrid soot.

cards.front: What does a smoking gun do at the pass?
cards.back: Blows cool smoke under a cloche or into a container for seconds or minutes: a seasoning for a plate, a liquid or a cocktail, never a preserver.

cards.front: What is a boucherie?
cards.back: A communal hog butchering in Cajun and Creole Louisiana, where neighbours turn a whole hog into boudin, cracklins and sausage, and what will not keep fresh is salted or smoked.

cards.front: Where does smoke appear on the Brennan's menus?
cards.back: In the tomato water of the Creole Tomato Tostada, the oyster dressing of the Creole Caesar, the potato pavé with the hanger steak and the Smoked Cauliflower.

cards.front: What must every guest hear about the Creole Caesar dressing?
cards.back: That it is made with smoked oysters; flag it on the ticket and take shellfish questions to the kitchen.

questions.q: Which of these is cold smoked, taking flavour without being cooked?
questions.answer: Smoked salmon, sliced thin
distractors: Tasso
Andouille
Smoked trout that flakes
questions.why: Cold smoking keeps the chamber below about 32°C (90°F), so salmon stays silky; tasso, andouille and flaking smoked trout are hot smoked and cook as they smoke.

questions.q: Why must fish be cured before it is cold smoked?
questions.answer: The smoke does not cook it, so salt protects it
distractors: The cure makes the smoke darker
Salt helps the wood smoulder
The cure shortens the smoking time to a few minutes
questions.why: Cold smoke stays below cooking heat and its warmth suits bacteria, so the salt cure, not the smoke, does the protecting.

questions.q: Which wood should never be used for smoking food?
questions.answer: Pine
distractors: Pecan
Hickory
Apple
questions.why: Resinous softwoods such as pine give a bitter, sooty smoke; pecan, hickory and apple are clean-burning hardwoods.

questions.q: What kind of smoke should a cook want from the smoker?
questions.answer: Thin and pale blue
distractors: Thick and white
Black and billowing
Grey and heavy
questions.why: Thin blue smoke comes from wood burning cleanly; thick white or dark smoke from a smothered fire coats food with acrid soot.

questions.q: Which of these is hot smoked, cooking through as it takes the smoke?
questions.answer: Tasso
distractors: Scottish smoked salmon
Smoked cheddar
A smoked cocktail
questions.why: Tasso, like andouille, cooks as it smokes; salmon and cheese are cold smoked for flavour alone, and a cocktail takes smoke from a gun.

questions.q: What is the pellicle, and why does it matter in smoking?
questions.answer: A dry, tacky skin that takes smoke evenly
distractors: A wet brine that keeps the fish moist in the smoke
A wood chip soaked in water
The ash left after the fire
questions.why: Smoke clings to a dry, tacky surface and colours a wet one patchily, so food is air-dried before it goes in.

questions.q: A guest orders the Creole Caesar. What must the server mention?
questions.answer: The dressing is made with smoked oysters
distractors: The lettuce is smoked over pecan
The croutons are smoked at the table to order
The cheese is cold smoked in house
questions.why: Guests do not expect oysters in a Caesar, so every guest hears it, the ticket is flagged and shellfish questions go to the kitchen.

questions.q: In south Louisiana, what is a boucherie?
questions.answer: A communal hog butchering
distractors: A smoked sausage shop
A Mardi Gras parade
A crawfish boil supper
questions.why: Neighbours work together to turn a whole hog into boudin, cracklins and sausage, and what will not keep fresh is salted or smoked to last.

entries.title: Frying and the fry station
entries.summary: Deep frying cooks food submerged in clean oil at about 170 to 190°C (338 to 374°F): surface water flashes to steam, the coating sets crisp, and the inside cooks gently in its own moisture.
entries.guest: Popcorn shrimp are bite-size Louisiana shrimp, fried golden and crunchy, with a tangy Crystal hot sauce gastrique, a sweet and sour sauce. Any coating or fryer question, I take to the kitchen.

paras: Deep frying is cooking food fully submerged in hot oil, usually about 170 to 190°C (338 to 374°F). The moment food goes in, the water at its surface boils into steam: that is the furious bubbling. Steam pushing outward keeps most of the oil out while the surface dries and browns into a crust, and inside, the food cooks gently in its own moisture. Get the heat right and fried food is crisp and light; get it wrong and it is greasy or burnt.

Oil that is too cool lets the bubbling slow before the crust sets, and the food soaks up fat. Oil that is too hot browns the outside before the inside cooks, and breaks down faster. Frying in a pan with less fat is shallow frying, taught with the sauté.

Coat it. Most fried food wears a coating that browns into the crust and protects what is inside. The standard breading, à l'anglaise in the classical kitchen (the same phrase also names plainly boiled vegetables), runs flour, egg wash and crumbs: flour dries the surface so the egg clings, and egg glues on the crumbs. Keep one hand for the dry and one for the wet. Louisiana often fries its seafood in a seasoned cornmeal dredge, often after a dip in egg, milk or buttermilk, and batter coats okra and onion rings. Let a breaded piece rest a few minutes so the coating sets.

Fry it. Fill the fryer to its line and heat the oil: about 175°C (347°F) suits most breaded seafood and vegetables, 180 to 190°C (356 to 374°F) small pieces and the second fry of French fries, and about 160°C (320°F) the first, blanching fry of potatoes. Fill the basket no more than half, lower it gently, and fry in small batches: every load drops the oil's heat, and an overloaded basket drops it so far that the food stews in fat. Let the oil recover between batches.

Drain and season. Lift the basket, shake it over the oil, and turn the food onto a rack, never onto paper, where it sits in its own steam and softens. Salt it at once, while the surface oil still holds the salt, and send it straight away: fried food is at its crispest in its first few minutes.

Care for the oil. Skim crumbs between batches, because they burn, darken the oil and flavour the next batch. Filter it at least daily, top it up with fresh oil, and keep salt and water away from it: salt speeds its breakdown, and water makes hot oil spit violently. Fresh oil is pale and smells clean. Change it when it turns dark, smells acrid or fishy, foams and will not settle, or smokes at its normal heat.

Shared oil carries what was fried in it. Shrimp, fish and anything coated in wheat flour or crumbs leave their proteins in the oil, and frying does not destroy them, so food cooked in shared oil can carry traces of what went before. Many kitchens give seafood its own fryer for flavour as well as for that reason, but no server can promise how tonight's fryers are set up: questions about shellfish, coatings, shared fryers and oil always go to the kitchen.

The fryer also burns. Lower food in gently and away from you, and never fill past the line. If the oil catches fire, never use water, which flashes to steam and throws burning oil out of the fryer: turn off the heat, smother it with a lid or the kitchen's class K extinguisher, made for cooking-oil fires, and call the chef.

At Brennan's the fryer works across the menus. The popcorn shrimp at the Roost are bite-size Louisiana shrimp fried golden, with a Crystal gastrique. The artichokes on the Eggs Sardou are cooked tender, then coated and fried crisp. The poussin is a Cornish hen brined in sweet tea, coated and fried before its mustard cream. Brabant potatoes are classically cubed, blanched or par-fried, fried golden and tossed in butter, garlic and parsley, with the house finish and fryer confirmed at lineup; good French fries are usually fried twice, and how the kitchen fries ours is a lineup question.
Fried food waits for no one: run it the moment it is up. Describe it by its crunch and by what is inside, and send every question about coatings, shared fryers or the oil to the kitchen, every time.

ratios.label: The standard breading
ratios.value: Flour, then egg wash, then crumbs

ratios.label: Egg wash
ratios.value: About 1 egg to 15 ml (1 tbsp) of milk or water, beaten smooth

ratios.label: The basket
ratios.value: No more than half full, fried in small batches

temps.label: Small pieces and the second fry of French fries
The top of the working range

faults.cause: Oil too cool, or a basket so full that the heat dropped.
faults.fix: Bring the oil back to temperature and fry smaller batches, letting it recover between them.

faults.cause: Oil too hot for the size of the piece.
faults.fix: Lower the heat, cut smaller, or blanch thick pieces at a lower heat first.

faults.cause: Wet food, no flour first, or moved before the crust set.
faults.fix: Pat dry, flour before the egg, rest the breading a few minutes and leave it alone in the oil.

faults.cause: Drained on paper, piled up or covered.
faults.fix: Drain on a rack in a single layer and send it uncovered.

faults.cause: Tired oil, burnt crumbs, or seafood fried in the oil for potatoes.
faults.fix: Skim and filter, change dark oil, and keep seafood to its own fryer where the kitchen sets one.

faults.fault: Oil foams and will not settle
faults.cause: Old or contaminated oil.
faults.fix: Change it.

brennans.how: Bite-size Louisiana shrimp, coated and fried quickly until golden, served at the Roost with a Crystal gastrique. The coating crisps while the shrimp stays sweet and tender; coating questions go to the kitchen.
Trimmed artichoke hearts are cooked tender, then coated and fried crisp, for crunch against the soft poached eggs and creamy spinach. Check the coating with the kitchen for any guest who asks.

The Cornish hen is brined in sweet tea, a Southern trick that usually means strong black tea, sugar and salt, then dried, coated and fried until the skin is crisp, and sauced with mustard cream. How long it brines is a question for the chef.
Cubed potatoes, blanched or par-fried, then fried golden and tossed in butter with garlic and parsley: the old New Orleans side. Confirm the house finish and the fryer at lineup.

Good fries are usually cooked twice: a lower first fry cooks the potato soft, a hotter second fry crisps and browns it, and salt goes on as they leave the oil. At the Roost they come with pink sauce; how ours are fried is a lineup question.

sources.title: A Guide to Modern Cookery, A. Escoffier (London: Heinemann, 1907)

cards.front: Why does deep-fried food turn crisp rather than greasy?
cards.back: Surface water flashes to steam that keeps the oil out while the coating dries and browns; the inside cooks gently in its own moisture.

cards.front: What is the working range of oil temperature for deep frying?
cards.back: About 170 to 190°C (338 to 374°F); most breaded seafood fries well near 175°C (347°F).

cards.front: What happens when the oil is too cool?
cards.back: The bubbling slows before the crust sets, so the food soaks up oil and comes out greasy and heavy.

cards.front: What happens when fryer oil runs too hot, and what puts out an oil fire?
cards.back: The outside burns before the inside cooks and the oil breaks down. Pushed further it smokes and can catch fire: turn off the heat and smother it with a lid or a class K extinguisher, never water.

cards.front: What is the standard breading, in order?
cards.back: Flour, egg wash, crumbs: flour dries the surface so the egg clings, and the egg glues on the crumbs.

cards.front: How does Louisiana usually coat seafood for frying?
cards.back: In a seasoned cornmeal dredge, often after a dip in egg, milk or buttermilk, for a gritty, golden crust.

cards.front: Why fry in small batches?
cards.back: Every load drops the oil's heat; an overloaded basket drops it so far that the food stews in fat instead of crisping.

cards.front: Why drain fried food on a rack and salt it at once?
cards.back: On paper it sits in its own steam and softens, and salt sticks only while the surface oil is still hot.

cards.front: When is fryer oil due for a change?
cards.back: When it is dark, smells acrid or fishy, foams and will not settle, or smokes at its normal heat.

cards.front: Why can a fryer carry traces of foods fried in it earlier?
cards.back: Shrimp, fish and breaded foods leave their proteins in shared oil, and frying does not destroy them, so every such question goes to the kitchen.

cards.front: Why are French fries fried twice?
cards.back: A lower first fry cooks the potato soft; a hotter second fry crisps and browns it. Salt goes on as they leave the oil.

cards.front: Which Brennan's plates come from the fryer, and how is the poussin readied for it?
cards.back: The popcorn shrimp, the crispy artichokes on the Eggs Sardou, Brabant potatoes, French fries and the poussin, a Cornish hen brined in sweet tea, then dried, coated and fried. Coating and fryer questions go to the kitchen.

questions.q: At about what oil temperature does most breaded seafood deep fry well?
questions.why: Most frying runs at about 170 to 190°C (338 to 374°F); cooler and the food turns greasy, hotter and the outside burns first.

questions.q: A basket of shrimp comes out pale, heavy and greasy. What is the likely cause?
questions.answer: The oil had cooled too far
distractors: The oil was far too hot
The shrimp were salted after frying
The coating rested before frying
questions.why: Cool oil, or a load big enough to drop its heat, lets the crust set late, so the food soaks up oil.

questions.q: What is the order of the standard breading for frying?
questions.answer: Flour, egg wash, crumbs
distractors: Egg wash, crumbs, flour
Crumbs, flour, egg wash
Flour, crumbs, egg wash
questions.why: Flour dries the surface so the egg clings, and the egg glues on the crumbs; out of order, the coating slides off.

questions.q: Where should fried food go as it comes out of the oil?
questions.answer: Onto a rack, salted at once
distractors: Onto kitchen paper, covered
Into a lidded hotel pan
In a pile in the basket
questions.why: On a rack, air reaches every side and steam escapes; on paper or under a lid it softens, and salt sticks only while the surface is hot.

questions.q: Which sign tells you the fryer oil needs changing?
questions.answer: It foams and will not settle
distractors: It is pale and smells clean
It bubbles hard when food goes in
It holds its set temperature
questions.why: Persistent foam, a dark colour, an acrid or fishy smell or smoke at normal heat all mean the oil has broken down; fresh oil is pale and clean.

questions.q: A guest asks whether the fries share oil with the shrimp. What does the server do?
questions.answer: Ask the kitchen and report back
distractors: Say frying removes any trace
Say the fries are cooked apart
Guess from the menu description
questions.why: Frying does not destroy proteins left in shared oil, and only the kitchen knows how tonight's fryers are set up, so the question goes there.

questions.q: Why are good French fries cooked in two separate fries?
questions.answer: A low fry cooks them, a hot fry crisps them
distractors: The first fry seasons the oil for the second
Twice makes them take less salt
The first fry crisps, the second softens the centre
questions.why: The first, lower fry cooks the potato soft inside; the second, hotter fry crisps and browns the outside, and salt goes on at once.

questions.q: Why does a cook fry in small batches rather than one full basket?
questions.answer: So the oil holds its heat
distractors: So each piece takes more coating
So the fryer uses less power
So the oil darkens more evenly
questions.why: Each load cools the oil; a small batch lets it stay near temperature and recover quickly, so the crust sets fast.

questions.q: What is done to the poussin of the Poussin à la Moutarde before it is fried?
questions.answer: It is brined in sweet tea
distractors: It is confited in duck fat
It is smoked over pecan
It is poached in stock
questions.why: A sweet tea brine, usually strong black tea, sugar and salt, seasons the Cornish hen and helps the skin brown; then it is dried, coated and fried.

questions.q: Oil at the fry station catches fire. What should you reach for?
questions.answer: A lid or the kitchen's class K extinguisher
distractors: A jug of cold water
A wet kitchen cloth
A scoop of ice from the bar
questions.why: Water flashes to steam under burning oil and throws the fire out of the fryer. A lid cuts off the air, and a class K extinguisher is made for cooking-oil fires.
